answer: Yes. The story uses sustained retail metaphors to explore class, identity, and belonging. The narrator feels “scanned and set aside in the bagging area,” while Miss Emily’s scrutiny is “an audit”—comparisons rooted in the narrator’s experience that also expose how people assign social value. “She was editing me, and you don’t edit a thing you plan to throw away” captures the ambiguous mixture of care and control in their relationship. These metaphors deepen characterization rather than merely decorating the prose.
